course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments in voting took place in the United States between 1800 and 1848?
choices: States extended the vote to women who owned property and to all free Black men in the North
Most states dropped property requirements, so nearly all adult white men could vote
Congress passed a law that required every state to grant the vote to all adult citizens
States raised property requirements, which reduced the number of men who could take part in elections
questions.explanation: As new western states entered the Union and older states revised their constitutions, property requirements for white men ended in most places.
choiceExplanations: Women could not vote anywhere in this period, and some states took the vote from free Black men.
As new western states entered the Union and older states revised their constitutions, property requirements for white men ended in most places.
Voting qualifications remained a matter for the states.
Property requirements were lowered or dropped in most states.
questions.distinguisher: The women and Black men choice is close because suffrage was a major reform topic, but the expansion in this period applied to white men.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The growth of factories, canals, and steamboats in the early 1800s is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A decline in foreign trade that forced farmers to raise crops for their own families only
A federal program that made every factory and canal the property of the national government
A drop in immigration that left American employers unable to hire workers in any city
An economic shift in which more Americans produced goods for sale in distant markets
questions.explanation: The market revolution replaced much household production with production for sale, and new transportation helped to link producers and consumers.
choiceExplanations: Trade and commercial production increased in this period.
Most factories and many canals were privately owned or built by the states.
Immigration to Northern cities increased in these decades.
The market revolution replaced much household production with production for sale, and new transportation helped to link producers and consumers.
questions.distinguisher: The foreign trade choice is close because trade disruptions affected merchants, but the long-term trend was toward more commercial production.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: How did the acquisition of lands in the West affect the politics of slavery between 1800 and 1848?
choices: It gave rise to contests over whether slavery would be allowed to spread into new territories
It ended the debate because every new territory was closed to slavery by federal law
It united the sections because the North and South agreed on the rules for new territories
It removed the issue from Congress because the territories alone decided about slavery
questions.explanation: Each new addition of land raised the question of whether slavery would spread, and Congress and the sections struggled over the answer.
choiceExplanations: Each new addition of land raised the question of whether slavery would spread, and Congress and the sections struggled over the answer.
Congress did not close every territory to slavery, and the debate grew.
The sections disagreed over the extension of slavery.
Congress took part in decisions about slavery in the territories.
questions.distinguisher: The closed-to-slavery choice is close because the Missouri Compromise banned slavery in part of the Louisiana Purchase, but it did not settle the issue.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes how many Americans worked to improve their society between 1800 and 1848?
choices: They relied mainly on federal agencies that Congress created to carry out reform programs
They withdrew from public life and avoided joining groups that tried to influence others
They formed voluntary organizations outside of government to change behavior and institutions
They waited for state legislatures to appoint boards that would carry out each reform
questions.explanation: Inspired by new religious and intellectual movements, many Americans joined voluntary associations for temperance, abolition, and women's rights.
choiceExplanations: Reformers worked mainly through private organizations and not federal agencies.
Many reformers formed groups and sought to influence public opinion.
Inspired by new religious and intellectual movements, many Americans joined voluntary associations for temperance, abolition, and women's rights.
Most reform groups began as private associations.
questions.distinguisher: The federal agencies choice is close because reformers sometimes asked for new laws, but their main work was done by voluntary groups.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why manufacturing and agricultural production expanded dramatically in the early 1800s?
choices: A permanent federal ban on imports that gave American farmers control of world markets
Canals, steamboats, and other new transportation enlarged the markets for goods
A fall in the size of the average farm, which raised the price of food in every region
A national tax on European goods that paid directly for the construction of every factory
questions.explanation: Canals, steamboats, and later railroads lowered the cost of moving goods and extended the reach of producers.
choiceExplanations: No permanent ban on imports gave American farmers control of world markets.
Canals, steamboats, and later railroads lowered the cost of moving goods and extended the reach of producers.
Production grew because markets expanded, not because farms became smaller.
Factories were mainly financed by private investors.
questions.distinguisher: The import ban choice is close because the Embargo Act briefly encouraged domestic manufacturing, but it did not give farmers control of world markets.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a goal of United States foreign policy in the early 1800s?
choices: Expanding the nation's borders and promoting foreign trade
Joining permanent military alliances with the leading European powers to defend American trade
Reducing trade with the rest of the world so that the nation could rely on its own farms
Acquiring overseas colonies in Asia and the Pacific in order to build a naval empire
questions.explanation: The United States tried to claim territory throughout North America and to promote foreign trade while avoiding European conflicts.
choiceExplanations: The United States tried to claim territory throughout North America and to promote foreign trade while avoiding European conflicts.
American leaders avoided permanent alliances with European powers.
The government sought to protect and increase foreign trade.
Overseas colonies in Asia came later, in the 1890s.
questions.distinguisher: The permanent alliance choice is close because the United States had been allied with France in the 1770s, but later policy avoided alliances.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The emergence of a new national culture in the early 1800s is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A European refusal to export books, art, and ideas to the United States after the War of 1812
A federal program that required every region to adopt a single set of customs and beliefs
A decline in religious life after the Revolution, which left few Americans with shared beliefs
A growing desire to define an American identity, shaped by European and Romantic ideas
questions.explanation: Americans wanted a culture of their own, but they drew on European Romanticism, liberal ideas, and regional traditions.
choiceExplanations: European books, art, and ideas continued to reach the United States.
Regions kept distinct cultures, and the federal government did not impose one.
Religious life grew in the early 1800s, especially during the Second Great Awakening.
Americans wanted a culture of their own, but they drew on European Romanticism, liberal ideas, and regional traditions.
questions.distinguisher: The European refusal choice is close because the war strained relations, but cultural and commercial ties continued.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the North and the South by the 1840s?
choices: The South built more canals and railroads than the North, which linked its farms to its factories
The North relied on enslaved labor for most work, while the South relied on wage labor
The North built factories, banks, and cities, while the South relied on exporting cotton
The South received most of the new immigrants, while the North attracted almost none
questions.explanation: Economic development encouraged the growth of different regions, with Northern industry and commerce and a Southern economy based on staple crops.
choiceExplanations: The North built far more canals and railroads than the South.
Slavery was concentrated in the South, and the North ended or reduced slavery.
Economic development encouraged the growth of different regions, with Northern industry and commerce and a Southern economy based on staple crops.
Most immigrants settled in the North and Midwest.
questions.distinguisher: The canals and railroads choice is close because both regions used transportation, but the North built much more of it.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why westward expansion increased tensions between the North and the South?
choices: Westerners refused to pay federal taxes that would finance roads and canals in the East
New territories raised the issue of slavery's spread and the balance of power in Congress
Northern manufacturers wanted to stop all western settlement in order to protect their workers
Southern planters wanted western lands for factories that the North had refused to build
questions.explanation: Admitting new states and organizing territories could shift the balance of free and slave states, so every addition of land raised the stakes for both sections.
choiceExplanations: The conflict between the North and South centered on slavery.
Admitting new states and organizing territories could shift the balance of free and slave states, so every addition of land raised the stakes for both sections.
Northern leaders did not seek to stop western settlement as a whole.
Southern planters sought western lands for farming and slave labor.
questions.distinguisher: The tax choice is close because westerners cared about federal spending, but the main sectional conflict concerned slavery.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.
